title: One Trillion for the Pentagon, and Wanting More. Less Than Half of One Percent for Humanity
author: Daniel Warner
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/04/IMG_3654-680x510.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/31/one-
trillion-for-the-pentagon-and-wanting-more-less-than-half-of-one-percent-for-
humanity/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/04/IMG_3654-680x510.jpg)

Photograph by Nathaniel St. Clair

The U.S. House of Representatives voted on July 22 to increase defense
spending by US$73 billion. At about the same time as the House vote, the
Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) announced
that it will be moving to a smaller building in Geneva because of budget cuts.

The contrast could hardly be starker. One decision expands America's capacity
to wage war; the other diminishes its capacity to save lives. "Without
immediate support, women and girls at extreme risk of rape and other abuse are
losing access to services that kept them safe. Children are being left without
teachers or schools, pushing them into child labour, trafficking or early
marriage. Refugee communities will have less shelter, water and food." UNHCR
High Commissioner Filippo Grandi warned in March 2025.

Under its mandate, UNHCR is responsible for 122 million refugees and
internally displaced people worldwide. The United States’ contribution to
UNHCR was around $2 billion in 2024, 40% of the voluntary funding. It has been
slashed to $868 million. More than 5,000 staff have been laid off.

At a time when one in every seventy people on Earth has been forced to flee,
what will an additional US$73 billion for the Pentagon do for those 122
million people?

UNHCR’s situation is part of a broader pattern of U.S. humanitarian cutbacks.
Under Donald Trump, Foreign Operations and Related Programs (which includes
development assistance, humanitarian aid, economic assistance, and much global
health funding) has fallen from roughly $36 billion to about $19 billion, a
47% cut. The result is an estimated US$3–4 billion annual reduction in U.S.
support for Geneva-based international organisations and the vulnerable people
they serve.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has had to shrink its program budget after
the U.S. announced it would leave the organization and reduce funding. The
organization is cutting its biennial budget by about 21%. The UN human rights
office (OHCHR) has suffered a near-100% reduction in U.S. voluntary funding.

Does all this matter?

Peer-reviewed studies published in The Lancet estimate that if the current
dismantling of U.S. foreign assistance continues, it could contribute to
around 14 million additional deaths by 2030, including more than 4.5 million
children. These are projections, not observed deaths, but they illustrate the
scale of what is at stake.

For UNHCR, for example, in Sudan and neighboring countries it means cash
assistance that allowed refugee families to buy food and pay rent has been
reduced or suspended for many households. For the WHO, it means reduced
support for disease surveillance, making it harder for countries to detect
outbreaks of diseases such as cholera, measles, and mpox early. For the OHCHR,
it means fewer human rights officers deployed in conflict-affected countries
and reduced monitoring of arbitrary detention, torture, and attacks on
civilians.

The effects are not limited to UN agencies. The consequences extend equally to
global HIV/AIDS programs coordinated through Geneva-based UNAIDS and supported
by the U.S.-funded PEPFAR initiative. Through PEPFAR, the United States has
helped save more than 26 million lives since 2003 and currently supports HIV
treatment for more than 20 million people. Yet UNAIDS warns that if
U.S.-funded HIV programs are permanently dismantled, the world could face 6.6
million additional HIV infections and 4.2 million additional AIDS-related
deaths between 2025 and 2029. Such a reversal would rank among the greatest
setbacks in the history of the global response to HIV/AIDS.

“In countries with a high level of HIV, funding for condom programming
declined by 93%, and funding for programmes that ensure people can reach
prevention services (e.g. supportive laws, regulations and policy
environments) reduced by 80%,” said UNAIDS.

Some may argue that none of this affects the United States or its citizens
directly, or even the country itself. Beyond humanitarianism as such, the
question is whether these savings are strategically meaningful. Pandemics do
not respect borders. COVID-19 demonstrated that a virus emerging thousands of
miles away can shut down the American economy within months. Weakening the
WHO's capacity to detect and respond to outbreaks early is therefore not
simply a problem for poorer countries.

The same applies to conflicts. Refugee crises, regional wars and state
collapse rarely remain local. They disrupt trade, energy markets and
migration, eventually affecting countries far removed from the original
crisis. The war with Iran in the Middle East is affecting gas prices
throughout the U.S.

Humanitarian cuts are often defended as unavoidable fiscal decisions. Every
dollar a government spends on "guns" (defense, military, and security) is a
dollar it cannot spend on "butter" (civilian goods and services such as
healthcare, education, infrastructure, or foreign aid). This is the classic
"guns versus butter" trade-off.

But that trade-off doesn’t hold now. For FY2026, the United States is expected
to spend about US$1 trillion on defense. The estimated US$3–4 billion
reduction in funding for Geneva-based humanitarian organisations amounts to
roughly 0.3–0.4% of that budget. Yet the United States is not fighting a
declared war. It is dismantling humanitarian institutions to save less than
half of one percent of what it spends on its military.

What do these choices say about American priorities? During the COVID-19
pandemic, the WHO played a pivotal role in global coordination. With the
likelihood of pandemics spreading, is gutting the WHO really in America’s
interests? A saving of $3–4 billion may appear large in isolation, but it is
almost invisible when viewed in the context of a trillion-dollar defense
budget. What is the U.S.willing to sacrifice for relatively small gains?

Finally, what kind of power does the United States want to be? Military power
and humanitarian leadership are two different forms of influence, hard and
soft power, the power to compel and the power to persuade. Since 1945, the
United States has exercised both.

That balance seems to be shifting. Reduced presence in the field to help the
vulnerable, tens of thousands of unemployed humanitarians around the world,
and symbolic empty offices in Geneva are reflections of the United States’
over–militarization.

Obsession with hard power is crowding out soft power. There is no longer a
balance between the two. Joseph Nye, who coined the term "soft power," was
Assistant Secretary of Defense for International Security Affairs under Bill
Clinton and received the Department of Defense Distinguished Service Medal. He
understood that America's influence rested not in choosing between hard and
soft power, but in their complementarity.

The House vote was more than a budget decision. It was a statement about what
the United States now values. Washington voted for another US$73 billion for
the already bloated Pentagon while cutting billions from the institutions that
keep refugees alive, contain epidemics, fight HIV/AIDS and defend human
rights. All this to save less than half of one percent of the defense budget.
That is an abandonment of American humanitarian leadership. Another tragic
chapter in the MAGA March of Folly.
